item.title: History, mathematics and physics: two cases of the inverse square law
item.description: arXiv:2611.16700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How did mathematicians of the past relate to history? What can we learn from their experience? It is a truism to say that all people are embedded in history. It impacts on them in ways that they may or may not realise. At the two extremes, some may be completely oblivious; others may deliberately set out to change the historical narrative and the course of history. In this chapter, I explore these questions through two case studies. Both are of eminent British mathematicians/physicists in the late 1800s and their handling of an inverse square law of force. Both case studies show ways in which these men were blind to the history of their subject, conscious of it but limited by it, or deliberately trying to use it. First, I look at William Thomson's and James Clerk Maxwell's attempts to establish the inverse square law of electrostatics in the 1850s to 1870s. I ask the question, why did Maxwell devote the last years of his life to editing the 100-year-old electrical researches of Henry Cavendish and repeating Cavendish's experimental verification of the inverse square law of electrostatic repulsion? Second, I discuss John Henry Poynting and Newton's law of gravitation in the 1880s and 1890s, asking why Poynting preferred to describe his experiments as measurements of the mean density of the Earth rather than of the gravitational constant.
item.dc:creator: Isobel Falconer

item.title: Gravitational observables from a post-Carrollian expansion
item.description: arXiv:2611.14644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Einstein gravity, with a few exceptions, only admits nonlocal observables. This feature is often attributed to diffeomorphism invariance, since a gravitational field can thereby locally be transformed away. We show this attribution to be incorrect by constructing infinitely many exact ultralocal Dirac observables in (velocity dominated aka electric) Carroll gravity. The latter describes Einstein gravity's ultrarelativistic limit, is fully diffeomorphism invariant, and of independent interest in a variety of contexts. Starting from these Carroll observables a systematic construction of Dirac observables for Einstein gravity is outlined. The resulting "post-Carrollian" expansion is organized by the number of spatial gradients or fractional inverse powers of Newton's constant, where each partial sum is local.
item.dc:creator: Max Niedermaier, Mahdi Sedighi Jafari

item.title: Physical Observables and Superselection
item.description: arXiv:2611.17051v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It is well-known that a physical state may be represented by a unit vector in a Hilbert space, whilst a physical observable may be represented by a self-adjoint operator on that same space. However, the introduction of a superselection rule on a Hilbert space imposes constraints such that not all self-adjoint operators can represent observables, which has further consequences for the states themselves as well as the physical processes that transform them. In this article, we review the concept of superselection from the view of how such rules would affect what we consider to be physical. Arguments for the existence of a superselection rule due to charge or possibly energy conservation are given and the emergence of effective superselection rules due to decoherence or the lack of a shared reference frame are also discussed.
item.dc:creator: Martin Paul Vaughan

item.title: What Can Actually Be Proved About the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen Paradox? Operational Consistency, Locality, and Quantum Completeness
item.description: arXiv:2604.13135v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) argument concerns whether accurate quantum predictions imply a complete description of physical reality. We distinguish predictive adequacy, operational no-signalling, EPR elements of reality, and ontological completeness. We formalize the EPR reality criterion using observable-, value-, and context-dependent predicates and prove that its incompleteness implication does not entail a prohibition on objectively stochastic origins of outcomes. A two-observable stochastic-source countermodel establishes this limited logical non-entailment, without addressing randomness generated at measurement or reproducing the full quantum assemblage. We illustrate the latter distinction using an established two-setting qubit steering inequality. For continuous variables, we derive inferred-variance and Gaussian-steering criteria for a stipulated instantaneous elastic-collision map, studying mass ratios, incident wave-packet spreading, covariance inflation, and readout noise. We distinguish losses of fixed-axis Reid violations from losses of optimized Gaussian steering. These results are conditional benchmarks, not predictions for the proposed finite-duration ion-collision apparatus, whose scattering dynamics and preparation and measurement parameters remain unspecified. We also show why uncertainty inequalities and exponential decay memorylessness alone do not establish intrinsic ontological randomness. The analysis delimits the logical and physical assumptions needed for claims about EPR completeness without proposing a new hidden-variable dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Miko{\l}aj Sienicki, Krzysztof Sienicki
